company: Bank of New York Mellon Corp

teaser.text: Bank of New York Mellon (BNY) is a financial-services company that earns much of its living by keeping investments, payments and market transactions organized. To see its business clearly, follow what it sells, how one dollar moves through it, and which customers pay for the work.

stock.meta_description: BNY's weighted forecast is $133.96 in October 2027 and $139.54 in October 2029; the range is $86.70 to $206.43.

blocks.heading: Where could BNY's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: BNY’s price could reach $139.54 in October 2029, but only if recurring fee growth, margins, buybacks and capital hold; the nearer outcome is $133.96 in October 2027. Management raised its October 2026 operating-leverage outlook to nearly 500 basis points, with revenue growth around the midpoint of 12%–13% and adjusted expense growth around the midpoint of 7%–8%.

The weighted forecast implies a 4% loss with dividends in October 2027 and a 4% gain in October 2029. Its cases assign 30% probability to the bear case, 50% to base and 20% to bull, with October 2029 outcomes ranging from $86.70 to $206.43.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for BNY?

paragraphs.text: The base assumes moderate earnings growth with substantial dividends and buybacks. That follows Q3 revenue growth of 12% and expense growth of 8%, alongside management’s 2026 revenue and expense outlook. The bear case adds credit losses and reduces capital returns. The bull case assumes stronger fee growth, operating leverage and earnings, while capital remains sufficient for heavier repurchases.

blocks.heading: How much cash does BNY really make?

paragraphs.text: Capital spending remains a real use of cash. BNY invests in premises, equipment and capitalized software, whose cost reaches expenses gradually through amortization. Stock-based compensation is also economically relevant because it gives employees a claim on the company, even when it does not immediately use cash.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for BNY?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio compares the share price with profit per share. The price-to-book ratio compares it with accounting equity, the capital belonging to shareholders. A premium to book value can make sense if BNY repeatedly earns more on that equity than investors require.

dividend.meta_description: BNY's dividend, cash coverage, payout outlook and current yield, with the full memo's business and risk analysis.
dividend.opening: BNY's declared dividend is $0.63 quarterly. From 2021 through 2025, BNY paid $20,242 million to shareholders against cumulative free cash flow of $20,078 million.
dividend.closing: The full memo also explains BNY's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does BNY pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends begin at the declared $0.63 quarterly rate. The base case therefore pays $2.52 per share in the first window and $2.80 in October 2028. It reaches $3.08 in October 2029. The bear case freezes at $2.52, while the bull case reaches $3.28.

blocks.heading: Is BNY's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: From 2021 through 2025, BNY paid $20,242 million to shareholders against cumulative free cash flow of $20,078 million. Free cash flow is usually cash left after operating needs and capital spending, but a bank constantly buys securities, takes deposits, issues debt and meets capital rules. That is why free cash flow was negative $782 million in 2024 even as shareholder payments continued.

Buybacks were the larger return. BNY repurchased $13,894 million of shares and paid $6,348 million in dividends during the period. In 2025, it paid $1,447 million in dividends and spent $3,535 million on repurchases. The diluted share count fell from about 788 million in 2023 to 717 million in 2025, so the buybacks reduced the number of shares dividing future profits. Whether they created value depends on the prices paid.

earnings.title: BNY earnings: guidance and what to watch
earnings.meta_description: BNY expects its next results on January 15, 2027; guidance centers on revenue growth outpacing expense growth, with capital in focus.
earnings.opening: BNY's next results are expected on January 15, 2027. For BNY, watch whether revenue continues to outpace expenses.
earnings.closing: The full BNY memo also covers BNY's business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: BNY raised its operating-leverage outlook to nearly 500 basis points in October, from 400 basis points in July. At the beginning of 2026, it expected slightly more than 100 basis points. Management now expects revenue, excluding specified unusual items, to grow around the midpoint of 12%–13%, while adjusted expenses should grow around the midpoint of 7%–8%.

Some performance was delivered. Fee revenue rose 6% in 2025, and adjusted operating leverage reached 411 basis points, meaning revenue grew faster than expenses. But the expense promise was less exact: the original outlook called for 1–2% growth excluding notable items, while the full-year presentation reported 3%. A fair judgment credits the strong execution without pretending every target was met.

blocks.heading: What do BNY's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: The September 2026 quarter extended BNY’s year-over-year improvement but fell short of June’s exceptionally strong result. Revenue, operating income and earnings per share all rose from the prior year, while the pre-tax margin declined sequentially.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in BNY's next results?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is the fourth quarter ending December 31, 2026. Investors should compare revenue and expense growth, then examine the 2027 budget when management publishes it. If spending rises again, BNY will need to show how much follows revenue and how much creates a permanently higher cost base.

The reader should separate three outcomes: a noncash goodwill charge, a legal settlement that consumes money and a capital constraint that limits buybacks or growth. Together, the next earnings report, legal disclosures and capital figures will show whether BNY’s ambitious plan is self-funding.
